intro: A packet is layers inside layers, like an envelope inside an envelope. Ethernet or Wi-Fi gets it across the local network; IP (v4 or v6) carries it from computer to computer, across routers; TCP or UDP delivers it to the right program on that computer (the port number says which); and the application's own protocol (DNS, HTTP, TLS, SMB…) is the message itself. The Packet details pane shows the same layers, outermost first, and the Protocol column names the innermost one ANTA recognised.
categories: The outer layers of almost every packet: the local network, and the addresses that carry a packet from one computer to another.
Ports name the program on each end. TCP is a reliable two-way conversation; UDP sends single messages.
How devices find each other by name, get an address when they join, and keep their clocks right.
Web pages, downloads and the apps that talk to web servers.
What keeps traffic private, and how computers prove who is logging in.
Sending and reading mail, and moving files. Several of these are old and unencrypted.
File sharing, directory lookups and remote administration in a Windows (Active Directory) network.
Programs talking to database servers: logins, queries and results.
Controlling computers and network equipment from elsewhere, and phone calls over the network.
What switches and routers say to each other to keep the network running.
Packets carried inside other packets, and headers that capture tools add.

protocols.name: Ethernet
protocols.what: The wired local network. Every frame carries two hardware (MAC) addresses: the network card that sent it and the next device it goes to. On your own network that's the other computer; for anything on the internet it's the router.
protocols.see: Source and destination MAC addresses, and the type of what's inside (IPv4, IPv6, ARP). It is the first layer in the Packet details pane.
protocols.watch: A MAC address only means something on the local network: a packet from the internet shows your router's MAC as its source. The first half of a MAC names the card's maker (Apple, Cisco, Intel…), which ANTA shows next to it.
try: broadcasts: frames sent to every device on the network

protocols.name: VLAN tag
protocols.what: A small tag in an Ethernet frame that says which virtual network (VLAN) it belongs to, so one switch can keep several separate networks apart (for example staff, guests and phones).
protocols.see: A VLAN ID between the Ethernet and IP layers.
protocols.watch: Captures from a switch's mirror port often carry tags. Traffic in a VLAN where it shouldn't be can mean a misconfigured port, or someone trying to hop between VLANs (two tags in one frame).

protocols.name: Wi-Fi
protocols.what: Wireless networking. A capture taken in monitor mode shows the Wi-Fi frames themselves: beacons that announce networks, devices probing for and joining networks, and data.
protocols.see: Beacon, probe, authentication, association and data frames; with a Radiotap header, the signal strength and channel too.
protocols.watch: On a protected network the data frames are encrypted with the network's key: ANTA shows that they exist, not what's inside. A burst of deauthentication frames can mean someone is knocking devices off the network.

protocols.name: ARP
protocols.what: How a computer finds the hardware (MAC) address that belongs to an IP address on the local network. It asks everyone "who has 10.0.0.1?" and the owner answers "10.0.0.1 is at aa:bb:cc:…".
protocols.see: Info lines like "Who has 10.0.0.1? Tell 10.0.0.5" and "10.0.0.1 is at …".
protocols.watch: Two different MACs answering for the same address, especially the router's, is ARP spoofing: a device putting itself in the middle of other people's traffic. ANTA raises an alert for it.

protocols.name: IPv4
protocols.what: The addresses (like 192.168.1.20) that get a packet from one computer to another, across routers and the internet. Almost everything else rides inside IP.
protocols.see: Source and destination addresses, the time-to-live (TTL, lowered by one at every router) and which protocol is inside (TCP, UDP, ICMP).
protocols.watch: 10.x.x.x, 172.16–31.x.x and 192.168.x.x are private addresses (your own network); the rest are on the internet. A starting TTL of 64 usually means Linux or macOS, 128 Windows, 255 network equipment.
try: everything to or from one address
multicast (sent to a group of listeners)

protocols.name: IPv6
protocols.what: The newer Internet Protocol, with much longer addresses (like 2001:db8::5). Most devices speak IPv4 and IPv6 side by side, often without anyone noticing.
protocols.see: Source and destination addresses and a hop limit. Addresses starting fe80: only work on the local link; fd or fc ones are private.
protocols.watch: IPv6 is easy to overlook: when hunting, check it too, because firewall rules and filters written for IPv4 may not cover it.

protocols.name: ICMP
protocols.what: Messages about the network itself: ping (echo request and reply), and errors such as "destination unreachable" or "time to live exceeded" that a router or computer sends back when a packet can't be delivered.
protocols.see: Echo (ping) request and reply; Destination unreachable, with the start of the packet that failed quoted inside.
protocols.watch: Pings to many addresses in a row is a sweep (someone mapping the network). Unreachable messages explain why a connection failed. Large or steady pings can hide data (an ICMP tunnel).

protocols.name: ICMPv6
protocols.full: Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6
protocols.what: ICMP for IPv6. It also does the jobs ARP and DHCP do for IPv4: neighbor discovery (finding a device's hardware address) and router advertisements (how devices learn their address and router).
protocols.see: Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement, Router Advertisement, echo request and reply.
protocols.watch: Router Advertisements from a device that isn't your router can redirect traffic through it, the IPv6 version of ARP spoofing.

protocols.name: IGMP
protocols.what: How a device tells the network it wants to receive a multicast group: one stream sent to many listeners, used by some video, discovery and streaming traffic.
protocols.see: Membership reports and queries.
protocols.watch: Normal background traffic on most networks.

protocols.name: TCP
protocols.ports: any: the port names the service (80 web, 443 HTTPS, 22 SSH, 445 file sharing…)
protocols.what: A reliable two-way conversation between two programs. It starts with a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), numbers every byte so nothing is lost or delivered out of order, and ends with FIN (or RST to abort).
protocols.see: Ports, the flags [SYN], [ACK], [FIN], [RST], sequence and acknowledgement numbers, and notes like [TCP Retransmission] or [TCP Zero Window] when something goes wrong.
protocols.watch: Retransmissions and duplicate ACKs mean lost packets (a slow or faulty link). An RST right after a SYN means nothing listens on that port. Many SYNs to many ports from one host is a port scan.
try: packets that had to be sent again

protocols.name: UDP
protocols.what: Single messages with no connection and no guarantee they arrive: fast and simple. Used where a lost message doesn't matter or is simply asked again: DNS lookups, voice and video calls, games, QUIC.
protocols.see: Source and destination ports and a length.
protocols.watch: Steady UDP to one internet address, UDP on unusual ports, or a lot of data on port 53 (DNS tunnelling) are worth a look.

protocols.name: DNS
protocols.what: The internet's phone book: it turns names like example.com into addresses. Almost every connection starts with a DNS lookup, so DNS shows where a device is about to go.
protocols.see: "Standard query 0x1a2b A example.com" and a response with the same number and the answer.
protocols.watch: Lookups of random-looking names that don't exist (NXDOMAIN) can be malware searching for its server (DGA). Very long names, or very many names under one domain, can be data being smuggled out (DNS tunnelling). ANTA alerts on both.
try: lookups of names containing a word

protocols.name: mDNS
protocols.what: DNS without a server, for the local network: devices announce themselves and find each other (printers, Chromecasts, AirPlay speakers, phones) by asking everyone at once.
protocols.see: Questions and answers for .local names and services such as _ipp._tcp.local (printers).
protocols.watch: Normal on home and office networks. It reveals device names and types, which ANTA uses for the asset inventory.

protocols.name: LLMNR
protocols.what: A Windows fallback for finding a name on the local network when DNS doesn't know it.
protocols.see: Queries sent to everyone on the network for a single name.
protocols.watch: Anyone on the same network can answer these falsely to catch Windows logins (LLMNR poisoning); many organisations turn it off.

protocols.name: NBNS
protocols.what: The old Windows way of finding computers by name on a local network.
protocols.see: Name queries and registrations such as "Name query NB DESKTOP-7<00>".
protocols.watch: Like LLMNR it can be answered falsely to steal logins, and it announces computer names to everyone.

protocols.name: DHCP
protocols.what: How a device gets its IP address, router and DNS server when it joins a network: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.
protocols.see: DHCP Discover, Offer, Request and ACK, often with the device's host name and vendor.
protocols.watch: A second DHCP server answering (rogue DHCP) can send devices to the wrong router or DNS server. The options a device asks for help tell its operating system, which ANTA uses for the inventory.
try: requests that give the device's name

protocols.name: DHCPv6
protocols.what: DHCP for IPv6: hands out addresses and DNS servers to devices on an IPv6 network.
protocols.see: Solicit, Advertise, Request and Reply messages.
protocols.watch: As with DHCP, an unexpected server answering is a warning sign.

protocols.name: NTP
protocols.what: Keeps computer clocks in sync. Accurate time matters more than it seems: Windows logins (Kerberos) fail when clocks drift, and logs from different machines can't be lined up.
protocols.see: Client requests and server replies with timestamps.
protocols.watch: Servers that should use an internal clock talking to the internet, or very large NTP replies (used to flood victims in reflection attacks).

protocols.name: HTTP
protocols.what: How web pages, files and APIs are fetched: a request (GET /page) and a response (200 OK, 404 Not Found…) with headers and a body. Plain HTTP is not encrypted: anyone on the path can read and change it.
protocols.see: "GET /path HTTP/1.1" and "HTTP/1.1 200 OK". The Files tab lists what was downloaded.
protocols.watch: Programs downloaded over plain HTTP, passwords in forms, User-Agents that are scripts rather than browsers, and requests straight to bare IP addresses. ANTA alerts on suspicious downloads.
try: requests with the program that sent them

protocols.name: HTTP/2
protocols.what: A faster version of HTTP that sends many requests at once over one connection, in binary frames. Browsers use it with most big sites, inside TLS, so it is only readable with your own TLS key log.
protocols.see: HEADERS and DATA frames, each on a numbered stream.
protocols.watch: The same things as in HTTP, once you have decrypted your own traffic (Decrypt TLS…).

protocols.name: QUIC
protocols.what: The newer transport for web traffic (HTTP/3): encrypted from the first packet, over UDP. Chrome and many apps use it for Google, YouTube, Facebook and other large sites.
protocols.see: Initial and Handshake packets (ANTA reads the server's name from the first one), then protected packets.
protocols.watch: Most of it can't be read; the server name in the first packet tells you where it went.

protocols.name: OCSP
protocols.what: How a browser checks that a website's certificate hasn't been revoked: a small request to the certificate authority.
protocols.see: A request and a response inside HTTP.
protocols.watch: Normal background traffic.

protocols.name: SSDP
protocols.what: How smart TVs, media servers, game consoles and routers announce themselves on a home network.
protocols.see: M-SEARCH questions and NOTIFY announcements, sent to everyone.
protocols.watch: Normal on home networks, and it reveals device types. A router that answers UPnP from the internet is a risk.

protocols.name: TLS
protocols.full: Transport Layer Security (the encryption in HTTPS)
protocols.what: The encryption under HTTPS and many other services. A handshake agrees on keys (the Client Hello names the website it wants: the SNI), then everything else is encrypted Application Data.
protocols.see: Client Hello, Server Hello, Certificate, then Application Data.
protocols.watch: The server name and the client's fingerprint (JA3 and JA4) are readable even though the data isn't: a fingerprint used by one machine only can be malware. Load your own key log (Decrypt TLS…) to read your own traffic.
try: Client Hellos, with the website's name
connections to sites with a word in their name

protocols.name: DTLS
protocols.what: TLS for UDP. Used by some VPNs, WebRTC video calls and IoT devices.
protocols.see: Client Hello, Server Hello, then encrypted records.
protocols.watch: As with TLS: the server name and fingerprints are readable, the data isn't.

protocols.name: SSH
protocols.what: Encrypted remote login and file copying (scp, sftp) for servers and network equipment. Only the version banner at the start is readable.
protocols.see: "SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6" banners, a key exchange, then encrypted packets.
protocols.watch: SSH to or from unexpected places, on unusual ports, or long-lived SSH sessions to the internet can be remote control or a tunnel.
try: the version banners (which software each side runs)

protocols.name: Kerberos
protocols.what: How Windows domain logins work: a user proves who they are to the domain controller and gets tickets to use other services, without the password crossing the network.
protocols.see: AS-REQ and AS-REP (logging in), TGS-REQ and TGS-REP (asking for a ticket to a service), and errors such as a wrong password.
protocols.watch: Many failed logins (password guessing), and one account asking for many service tickets at once (Kerberoasting).
try: errors (wrong password, unknown user, clock skew…)

protocols.name: NTLM
protocols.what: The older Windows login method, still common: a challenge from the server and a response computed from the password, carried inside SMB, HTTP or other protocols.
protocols.see: NTLMSSP_NEGOTIATE, NTLMSSP_CHALLENGE and NTLMSSP_AUTH, the last with the user, domain and computer name.
protocols.watch: NTLM responses can be cracked offline or relayed to another server. NTLM logins from unexpected machines, or to the internet, are worth a look.

protocols.name: SMTP
protocols.what: How email is sent: from a mail program to its mail server, and between mail servers.
protocols.see: Client commands (EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA) and server replies (250 OK).
protocols.watch: Logins and messages in clear text without STARTTLS, and a workstation sending lots of mail directly to the internet (spam or malware).

protocols.name: POP3
protocols.what: An older way for a mail program to download email from a server.
protocols.see: USER, PASS, LIST, RETR commands and +OK replies.
protocols.watch: Logins in clear text on port 110: Statistics → Cleartext logins lists them.

protocols.name: IMAP
protocols.what: How mail programs read email that stays on the server: folders, read flags, and syncing between devices.
protocols.see: Tagged commands such as "a1 LOGIN", "a2 SELECT INBOX" and their replies.
protocols.watch: Logins in clear text on port 143.

protocols.name: FTP
protocols.what: An old way of transferring files: commands on port 21 (USER, PASS, RETR to download, STOR to upload) and each file on a separate data connection.
protocols.see: "Request: USER alice", "Response: 230 Logged in", "Request: STOR backup.tar".
protocols.watch: Passwords and files cross the network unencrypted. Uploads of configuration backups or programs: ANTA lists the files under Files and alerts on sensitive ones.

protocols.name: FTP data
protocols.ports: TCP (a port agreed for each transfer)
protocols.what: The separate connection that carries an FTP file or directory listing.
protocols.see: The file's bytes; the FTP command connection says what the file is.
protocols.watch: The Files tab rebuilds these files and hashes them.

protocols.name: SMB
protocols.what: Windows file sharing (shared folders and printers) and much of Windows remote administration. SMB2 and SMB3 are current; SMB1 is old and unsafe.
protocols.see: Negotiate, Session Setup (logging in), Tree Connect to \\server\share, then Create, Read and Write of files.
protocols.watch: Programs copied to ADMIN$ or C$ shares (how attackers spread between machines), SMB1 still in use, and many failed logins. ANTA lists the files copied and alerts on programs.

protocols.name: NetBIOS browser
protocols.full: NetBIOS datagrams and the Windows Browser protocol
protocols.what: Old Windows announcements: computers broadcasting their name, workgroup and role so they appear in the network neighbourhood.
protocols.see: Host Announcement and Domain/Workgroup Announcement messages.
protocols.watch: They reveal computer names and Windows versions, which ANTA uses for the inventory.

protocols.name: LDAP
protocols.what: How programs look up and change the directory: the users, groups and computers in Active Directory.
protocols.see: bindRequest (logging in), searchRequest, and searchResEntry results.
protocols.watch: Simple binds send passwords in clear text on port 389. Huge searches for every user and group can be an attacker mapping the domain.

protocols.name: CLDAP
protocols.what: LDAP over UDP: how Windows computers find their domain controller (the "LDAP ping").
protocols.see: A search for the domain and the domain controller's answer.
protocols.watch: The answers name the domain and its controllers, which ANTA shows on the network map.

protocols.name: DCE/RPC
protocols.full: Distributed Computing Environment / Remote Procedure Call
protocols.ports: TCP 135 and others, or inside SMB
protocols.what: How Windows programs call functions on another computer: managing services, users, scheduled tasks, the registry and replication. The endpoint mapper (port 135) says which port each service listens on.
protocols.see: Bind, then Request and Response with the interface and operation named (SAMR, LSARPC, SVCCTL, DRSUAPI…).
protocols.watch: Remote service creation (SVCCTL) or scheduled tasks (ATSVC) from a workstation, and replication requests (DRSUAPI) from a computer that isn't a domain controller (DCSync), are classic attacker moves.

protocols.name: MySQL
protocols.what: The MySQL / MariaDB database protocol: logins, queries and results.
protocols.see: The server's greeting, the login, queries such as "Request Query" and their results or errors.
protocols.watch: Databases reachable from workstations or the internet, queries in clear text, and bursts of errors from failed logins or injection attempts.

protocols.name: PostgreSQL
protocols.what: The PostgreSQL database protocol: logins, queries and results.
protocols.see: Startup, authentication, Simple Query and its rows or an error.
protocols.watch: As for any database: who can reach it, and errors in bursts.

protocols.name: SQL Server
protocols.what: Microsoft SQL Server's protocol: logins, SQL batches and results.
protocols.see: Pre-login, Login, SQL batch and the results or error messages.
protocols.watch: As for any database: who can reach it, and errors in bursts.

protocols.name: Telnet
protocols.what: Remote login with no encryption at all: everything typed, passwords included, crosses the network readable. SSH replaced it, but it lingers on old network equipment and IoT devices.
protocols.see: Option negotiation, then the text both sides type and print.
protocols.watch: Any Telnet is worth fixing. Its logins appear under Statistics → Cleartext logins.

protocols.name: RDP
protocols.what: Remote Desktop: seeing and controlling a Windows computer's screen over the network.
protocols.see: A connection request, then (usually) TLS-encrypted data.
protocols.watch: RDP from the internet, or from one workstation to many others (an attacker moving around the network).

protocols.name: SNMP
protocols.what: How network equipment is monitored and managed: counters, settings, alarms. Versions 1 and 2c are protected only by a "community string" sent in clear text.
protocols.see: get-request, get-response and trap messages.
protocols.watch: The factory-default communities public and private, and SNMP reachable from the internet. Statistics → Cleartext logins flags default communities.

protocols.name: SIP
protocols.what: Sets up voice and video calls over the network: who is calling whom. The sound itself travels separately (RTP).
protocols.see: INVITE, 180 Ringing, 200 OK, BYE.
protocols.watch: Many INVITE or REGISTER attempts from one address can be someone trying to make free calls through your phone system.

protocols.name: STP
protocols.what: How switches avoid loops (traffic going round in circles forever) by agreeing which links to keep switched off.
protocols.see: Configuration BPDUs every couple of seconds from switches.
protocols.watch: Topology changes over and over mean an unstable network; STP from a desk port can mean someone plugged in their own switch.

protocols.name: LLDP
protocols.what: Devices telling their direct neighbours what they are: switch name, port, model and management address.
protocols.see: Announcements every 30 seconds or so.
protocols.watch: It reveals the network's layout: handy for mapping, and for an attacker too.

protocols.name: CDP
protocols.what: Cisco's own version of LLDP: devices announcing their name, model and software to their neighbours.
protocols.see: Announcements from Cisco equipment.
protocols.watch: The software versions it announces tell an attacker which flaws to try.

protocols.name: GRE
protocols.what: Wraps one packet inside another to carry it across a network: site-to-site tunnels, and ERSPAN, which copies traffic to a capture point.
protocols.see: An outer IP header and GRE, then the original packet inside.
protocols.watch: Tunnels nobody set up can carry traffic past firewalls.

protocols.name: VXLAN
protocols.what: Carries whole Ethernet frames inside UDP, joining virtual networks in data centres and clouds.
protocols.see: An outer packet to port 4789 with another Ethernet frame inside.
protocols.watch: Mostly data-centre plumbing.

protocols.name: Geneve
protocols.what: A newer, more flexible relative of VXLAN used by cloud networks (and by AWS traffic mirroring).
protocols.see: An outer packet to port 6081 with another frame inside.
protocols.watch: Mostly cloud plumbing.

protocols.name: MPLS
protocols.what: Labels that internet providers' networks put on packets to send them quickly along set paths.
protocols.see: One or more labels between Ethernet and IP.
protocols.watch: Mostly provider plumbing.

protocols.name: PPPoE
protocols.what: How many DSL and fibre connections log in to the internet provider: a PPP session carried over Ethernet.
protocols.see: A session header and PPP, then IP inside.
protocols.watch: Seen in captures taken between a home router and the provider.

protocols.name: Linux cooked capture
protocols.what: Not a network protocol: what Linux records instead of an Ethernet header when capturing on the "any" interface. It says which way each packet went and on which interface.
protocols.see: The packet type (incoming, outgoing, broadcast) and the interface.
protocols.watch: Nothing to worry about: it just means the capture was taken with tcpdump -i any or similar.

protocols.name: Radiotap
protocols.what: Not sent on the network: the Wi-Fi card's own notes about each frame it captured (signal strength, channel, data rate).
protocols.see: Signal strength in dBm, the channel's frequency and the rate.
protocols.watch: Signal strength helps tell how near a transmitting device is.

protocols.name: Data
protocols.what: The bytes of a packet that ANTA (like Wireshark) has no decoder for: a custom or proprietary protocol, encrypted data, or a known protocol on an unusual port.
protocols.see: A Data layer with the raw bytes.
protocols.watch: Unknown traffic on common ports (443 especially) can be malware speaking its own protocol. Explain… says what the bytes most likely are, and ANTA alerts on non-TLS traffic on TLS ports.
